question: For decades this Caribbean island punched absurdly above its weight in amateur boxing, producing Olympic legends like Teófilo Stevenson and Félix Savón, both of whom turned down fortunes to turn professional. Which country?

options.info: Its state-run amateur programme made it the most successful Olympic boxing nation outside the United States, with Stevenson and Savón each winning three golds.
A Caribbean sporting powerhouse too, but its reputation rests on baseball rather than boxing.
Has produced world-class professional boxers such as Félix Trinidad, but not this amateur dynasty.
Better known for sprinting and cricket than for Olympic boxing dominance.

question: Long before Europeans arrived, communities in the Great Lakes and St. Lawrence region played a stick-and-ball game they called 'the Creator's game', sometimes with hundreds of players and goals kilometres apart. Which people gave the world the ancestor of modern lacrosse?

options.info: Their version, baggataway or tewaarathon, was both a sport and a spiritual practice; a Haudenosaunee national team still competes internationally today.
Arctic peoples developed their own athletic traditions, but not this stick-and-ball game.
A Southwestern nation with strong running traditions, far from the game's Great Lakes homeland.
Played a famous rubber-ball court game in Mesoamerica, but a completely different sport with no sticks.

question: Picture volleyball played with the feet, knees, chest and head over a waist-high net, with a ball woven from rattan and spectacular overhead bicycle-kick spikes. Sepak takraw is a national obsession in which Southeast Asian country, whose name provides the 'sepak' half of the sport's official title?

options.info: The modern name combines the Malay 'sepak' (kick) with the Thai 'takraw' (woven ball); Malaysia and Thailand jointly codified the sport in the 1960s.
Plays its own foot-shuttlecock game, đá cầu, which is related in spirit but a different sport.
Has a version called sipa, but the international sport's name and rules came from elsewhere.
Plays the circle game chinlone, non-competitive and without a net.

question: He won three Formula 1 world titles, was famous for almost supernatural qualifying laps in the wet, and his death at Imola in 1994 triggered the sport's biggest ever safety overhaul. Who was he?

options.info: The Brazilian's fatal crash at the 1994 San Marino Grand Prix, a day after Roland Ratzenberger's, led directly to modern F1 safety standards.
Another three-time Brazilian world champion, but he retired safely in 1991.
The Frenchman was this driver's greatest rival, winning four titles of his own.
A Canadian driver also killed in a qualifying crash, in 1982, but he never won a world title.

question: Between 1999 and 2017 one player collected 23 Grand Slam singles titles, the most by anyone in the Open Era, and won the Australian Open while in the early weeks of a pregnancy. Who?

options.info: Her 2017 Australian Open title, won while pregnant, was her 23rd and final major singles trophy.
Holds 22 majors and the only 'Golden Slam', but her career ended in 1999.
Won seven singles majors and many doubles titles alongside her sister.
Won 18 singles majors and a record haul in doubles, mostly in the 1970s and 80s.

question: In the late 1960s a director spent years researching a biopic so obsessively that his team assembled tens of thousands of index cards on his subject's daily life — then the studio pulled the plug after a rival Napoleon film flopped, and the project became cinema's most famous unmade movie. Which director?

options.info: His 'Napoleon' was researched down to costume swatches and troop movements but never shot; the material later fed into 'Barry Lyndon'.
Made sweeping historical epics like 'Lawrence of Arabia', and had unrealised projects of his own, but not this one.
Left behind several famously unfinished films, including 'The Other Side of the Wind', but no Napoleon project of this scale.
Spent years developing an unmade epic about the siege of Leningrad, a different abandoned passion project.

question: In the late 1990s Warner Bros. developed a Superman film with Tim Burton directing and a script by Kevin Smith. Costume tests were shot, tens of millions were spent, and then it collapsed — leaving behind photos of one very surprising actor in a long-haired Superman suit. Who was cast as the Man of Steel?

options.info: 'Superman Lives' died in pre-production in 1998; the surviving costume-test images of him became internet legend, and he later voiced Superman in an animated film.
Was considered for superhero roles in that era and later played Robotman, but never wore this suit.
Played Superman in the original films of 1978-87, long before this abandoned project.
Eventually played the role in 2006's 'Superman Returns', a completely separate production.

question: In 2012 a quietly devastating drama about a Tehran couple's separation, an ailing father with dementia and a disputed miscarriage won Iran its first Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film. Who directed it?

options.info: 'A Separation' won the Oscar in 2012, and he won a second for 'The Salesman' in 2017.
The elder statesman of Iranian cinema, winner of the Palme d'Or for 'Taste of Cherry', but he never won this award.
An acclaimed Iranian director known for films made under a state filmmaking ban, such as 'Taxi'.
Directed 'Children of Heaven', the first Iranian film ever nominated in this category, but it didn't win.

question: It began in 1987 as crude filler shorts on a variety show, went to its own series two years later, and is now the longest-running scripted primetime series in American television history. Who created this yellow-skinned family?

options.info: He sketched the family in a lobby minutes before pitching, naming most of them after his own relatives; the shorts ran on 'The Tracey Ullman Show'.
Created 'Family Guy' a decade later, an animated sitcom clearly influenced by this one.
Created 'Beavis and Butt-Head' and 'King of the Hill' for the same broadcaster, but not this show.
Co-created 'South Park' in 1997, a much later animated satire.

question: Working with a tiny crew, non-professional actors and no completed script, a Bengali graphic designer shot his first feature at weekends over three years, funding it partly by pawning his wife's jewellery. The result, about a village boy named Apu, stunned Cannes in 1956. Who was he?

options.info: 'Pather Panchali' launched the Apu Trilogy and Indian arthouse cinema's international reputation; he later received an honorary Academy Award.
A contemporary Bengali director known for films about Partition, but not this trilogy.
Another leading figure of parallel Indian cinema, active in the same decades.
Made lyrical Hindi classics like 'Pyaasa' in Bombay, a very different filmmaking world.

question: Listen to the clip below. This slow, deliberately plain piano piece was written in 1888 by a Parisian eccentric who worked as a cabaret pianist, owned a wardrobe of identical grey velvet suits, and later invented the idea of 'furniture music' meant to be ignored. Who wrote it?

audio.credit: Performed by Robin Alciatore — public domain recording via Wikimedia Commons

options.info: The first of his three 'Gymnopédies', marked 'lent et douloureux' — slow and painful. He kept dozens of identical grey suits and founded his own one-member church.
A close friend who orchestrated two of these pieces, which is partly why they are sometimes misattributed to him.
Another French composer of the era, famous for 'Boléro', but this isn't his work.
Wrote delicate French piano and chamber music in the same period, including a well-known Requiem.

question: Listen to the clip below — a breathless orchestral interlude written to accompany a magical transformation in an opera based on a Pushkin tale, which promptly escaped the opera house to become a showpiece for virtuosos on every instrument imaginable. Which Russian composer wrote it?

audio.credit: Performed by the United States Army Band — public domain recording via Wikimedia Commons

options.info: 'Flight of the Bumblebee' comes from his opera 'The Tale of Tsar Saltan', where a prince is turned into an insect to fly across the sea.
A fellow member of the Russian 'Mighty Handful', best known for 'Pictures at an Exhibition'.
Another of the 'Mighty Handful' — and a working research chemist — but not the composer of this piece.
A later Russian composer whose 'Peter and the Wolf' also assigns creatures to instruments, but from the 20th century.

question: Listen to the clip below. Published in 1899 and named after a social club in Sedalia, Missouri, this syncopated piano piece sold hundreds of thousands of copies of sheet music and made its African-American composer the acknowledged 'King of Ragtime'. Who wrote it?

audio.credit: Piano roll transfer of 'Maple Leaf Rag' — public domain recording via Wikimedia Commons

options.info: 'Maple Leaf Rag' earned him a royalty of one cent per copy and lifelong fame; his opera 'Treemonisha' won him a posthumous Pulitzer in 1976.
A New Orleans pianist who bridged ragtime and early jazz, and famously claimed to have invented jazz himself.
A stride pianist and entertainer of a later generation, known for 'Ain't Misbehavin''.
A genuine ragtime composer of the same era, often ranked just behind the correct answer, but not the writer of this piece.

question: Watch the clip below. This 1985 synth-pop hit only became a worldwide number one on its third release, after the label paid for a video mixing live action with thousands of hand-drawn pencil-sketch frames. Which Norwegian band recorded it?

audio.credit: a-ha – 'Take On Me' official video, via the a-ha channel on YouTube

options.info: 'Take On Me' flopped twice before the rotoscoped video by Steve Barron turned it into a global smash for the Oslo trio.
A Swedish, not Norwegian, pop duo whose big hits came a few years later.
Another Swedish act, and a 1990s phenomenon rather than a mid-80s one.
An English synth-pop duo active in the same era, but not the makers of this record.

question: Watch this cover version from 2002, recorded by an ailing country legend near the end of his life and widely considered to eclipse the original. Which band wrote and first released the song, on a bleak 1994 concept album?

audio.credit: Cover: Johnny Cash – 'Hurt', via JohnnyCashVEVO on YouTube — original song by Nine Inch Nails

options.info: Trent Reznor wrote 'Hurt' for 'The Downward Spiral' and said that after hearing this cover, the song no longer felt like his.
A Seattle band of the same era with a similarly bleak streak, but not the writers of this song.
The country legend also covered one of their songs, 'Personal Jesus', but that's a different track.
Known for harrowing songs about addiction in the same years, though not this one.

question: This French electronic duo spent two decades refusing to show their faces, appearing only as a pair of robots in gold and silver helmets, and explained the personas with a story about a studio accident on 9 September 1999. Who were they?

options.info: Thomas Bangalter and Guy-Manuel de Homem-Christo kept the helmets on from 2001 until the duo announced its split in 2021.
A later French electronic duo who used a glowing cross as their emblem rather than costumes.
A French duo from the same 'French touch' scene, but they performed without disguises.
British big-beat pioneers known for elaborate live visuals, not for hiding their identities.

question: From 1973 each member of this American rock band performed in black-and-white face paint as a fixed character: the Demon, the Starchild, the Spaceman and the Catman. Which band?

options.info: Gene Simmons was the Demon, Paul Stanley the Starchild, Ace Frehley the Spaceman and Peter Criss the Catman; they performed unmasked from 1983 to 1996.
Pioneered theatrical shock rock with heavy stage makeup, but as a single frontman persona rather than four characters.
A much later band whose members wear individual masks and are identified by numbers instead.
An avant-garde group famous for anonymity behind giant eyeball masks, not face paint characters.

question: This Italian composer left an opera unfinished at his death in 1924; at its premiere the conductor Toscanini stopped the orchestra mid-scene, turned to the audience and said the master had laid down his pen there. Which composer, whose other works include 'La Bohème' and 'Tosca'?

options.info: He died before completing 'Turandot'; the aria 'Nessun dorma' comes from it, and the opera was finished by Franco Alfano.
Wrote 'Pagliacci' in the same verismo tradition, but he died in 1919 and left no such famous fragment.
Best known for the one-act 'Cavalleria rusticana', often staged as a double bill with 'Pagliacci'.
An earlier Italian opera composer who wrote 'The Barber of Seville' and then largely stopped composing operas at 37.

question: A keen amateur astrologer, this English composer built a seven-movement orchestral suite around the astrological characters of the planets — 'the Bringer of War', 'the Bringer of Jollity' and so on — and pointedly left out the Earth. Who was he?

options.info: 'The Planets' (1916) was inspired by astrology rather than astronomy, which is why Earth is absent and Pluto was never added by him.
A close friend and fellow English composer, known for 'The Lark Ascending', but not this suite.
Wrote the 'Enigma Variations' and 'Pomp and Circumstance' marches, a generation earlier.
A later English composer whose orchestral showpiece is 'The Young Person's Guide to the Orchestra'.

question: Born in Baghdad and trained as a mathematician before turning to architecture, she designed swooping, curved buildings once dismissed as unbuildable and in 2004 became the first woman to win the Pritzker Prize. Who was she?

options.info: Her projects include the London Aquatics Centre, the Heydar Aliyev Center in Baku and the Bergisel ski jump in Innsbruck.
A Japanese architect who shared the Pritzker in 2010 as half of the practice SANAA.
An influential architect and theorist controversially left off her partner's 1991 Pritzker award.
A French architect known for bold, dark, sculptural buildings, but not a Pritzker laureate.

question: He called his New York studio 'the Factory', turned soup cans and celebrity headshots into silkscreen prints, and managed a band while making films in which almost nothing happens for hours. Who was he?

options.info: The leading figure of American Pop Art, he also produced The Velvet Underground and survived being shot in 1968.
The other great American Pop artist, working from comic-book panels and Ben-Day dots.
Painted flags and targets in the run-up to Pop Art, but worked in a very different, painterly way.
Made 'combines' merging painting and found objects, a bridge between Abstract Expressionism and Pop.

question: Searching ancient Chinese medical texts in the 1970s for a malaria treatment, one researcher found a 4th-century note about steeping sweet wormwood in cold water — and realised heat was destroying the active compound. Her extraction of artemisinin has since saved millions of lives. Who was she?

options.info: She won the 2015 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, the first Chinese woman to win a Nobel in the sciences, and tested the drug on herself first.
A Chinese-American physicist whose experiment disproved the conservation of parity, in a completely different field.
Not a scientist at all — a confusion with the cellist Yo-Yo Ma.
A French virologist who shared a Nobel for the discovery of HIV, not this antimalarial.

question: A 9th-century scholar at Baghdad's House of Wisdom wrote a book on 'al-jabr', solving equations by balancing both sides — and a Latin mangling of his own name later became the word for a step-by-step computational procedure. Who was he?

options.info: 'Algebra' comes from the title of his treatise and 'algorithm' from the Latinisation of his name, Algoritmi.
A Persian polymath whose 'Canon of Medicine' dominated European medical teaching for centuries.
A brilliant scholar who measured the Earth's radius with remarkable accuracy, but not the source of these two words.
Solved cubic equations geometrically and wrote celebrated poetry, but lived two centuries later.

question: In the 1970s an American astronomer measured how fast stars orbit at the edges of spiral galaxies and found they were moving far too quickly to be held in by visible matter alone — strong evidence for something invisible. Who was she?

options.info: Her galaxy rotation curves provided the first widely accepted evidence for dark matter; many argued she should have received a Nobel Prize.
Discovered the first radio pulsars in 1967, a different landmark that also famously bypassed her for a Nobel.
Her early-1900s work on variable stars gave astronomers a way to measure cosmic distances.
Classified hundreds of thousands of stellar spectra and devised the system still used today.

question: Between 1856 and 1863 an Augustinian friar in Brno crossbred some 28,000 pea plants, tracking traits like seed colour and pod shape, and worked out the mathematical rules of inheritance — which the scientific world then ignored for 35 years. Who was he?

options.info: His 1866 paper on inherited traits was rediscovered around 1900 and became the foundation of modern genetics.
One of the botanists who independently rediscovered these laws around 1900 and gave the original credit.
Established that genes sit on chromosomes, using fruit flies, decades later.
Devised the system for naming and classifying species, a century earlier and unrelated to heredity.

question: Placed under house arrest in 11th-century Cairo after failing to dam the Nile, one scholar used the time to write a 'Book of Optics', showing by experiment that we see because light enters the eye — not because rays shoot out of it. Who was he?

options.info: Often called a founder of the experimental method, he also described the camera obscura in detail; the Latin West knew him as Alhazen.
A Persian physician and alchemist who wrote a landmark treatise distinguishing smallpox from measles.
An Andalusian philosopher famous for commentaries on Aristotle, not for optics experiments.
An English friar who built on this scholar's optical work in the following century.

question: Roughly 9,300 kilometres long and taking about a week end to end, this railway line links Moscow with a Pacific port and crosses eight time zones. What is it called?

options.info: Completed in stages between 1891 and 1916, it runs from Moscow to Vladivostok and remains the longest railway line in the world.
A famous long-distance passenger service, but a European one running from Paris towards Istanbul.
An extraordinary Chinese line reaching over 5,000 metres altitude, but far shorter.
Spans a continent too, but connects eastern Canada with the Pacific coast at Vancouver.

question: Opened in 1869 after ten years of digging, this sea-level waterway spared ships the long haul around a whole continent — and a 2021 blockage by a single wedged container ship briefly held up a tenth of global trade. Which waterway?

options.info: Linking the Mediterranean and the Red Sea, it saves the voyage around the Cape of Good Hope; the Ever Given blocked it for six days in March 2021.
A vital natural shipping chokepoint in Southeast Asia, but not an artificial canal.
A busy German canal connecting the North Sea and the Baltic, on a much smaller scale.
A narrow Greek cut through solid rock, too tight for modern cargo ships.

question: Some weather stations here have gone decades without measurable rain, and NASA has used its terrain to test Mars rovers — yet it hosts the world's great observatories precisely because the skies are so reliably clear. Which desert?

options.info: Stretching along northern Chile between the Andes and the Pacific, it is the driest non-polar desert on Earth and home to the ALMA and Paranal observatories.
A cold desert across Mongolia and northern China, famous for dinosaur fossil beds.
Holds the record for the highest reliably measured air temperature, but is far wetter than this desert.
A vast sand desert in western China ringed by oases of the old caravan routes.

question: Its shore sits about 430 metres below sea level, making it the lowest exposed land on Earth, and its water is so salty that swimmers float on the surface and almost nothing lives in it. Which body of water?

options.info: Bordered by Jordan, Israel and the West Bank, it is shrinking by roughly a metre a year as the Jordan River is diverted.
The world's largest inland body of water, also below sea level but only mildly saline in most parts.
A hypersaline Utah lake that is also shrinking, but sits well above sea level.
A saline crater lake in Djibouti — Africa's lowest point, and genuinely saltier, but higher than this one.

question: In August 1947 the departing British drew a hastily agreed boundary line across the subcontinent, triggering one of the largest mass migrations in history. Which new state was created alongside independent India, initially in two wings separated by 1,600 kilometres of Indian territory?

options.info: Its eastern wing broke away in 1971 to become Bangladesh; the boundary was drawn by Cyril Radcliffe, who had never visited India before.
Did not exist in 1947 — it emerged in 1971 out of the eastern half of the correct answer.
Then called Ceylon, it gained independence separately in 1948 and was not part of this partition.
Then Burma, it was separated from British India in 1937 and became independent in 1948.

question: One of the most isolated inhabited places on Earth, roughly 3,500 kilometres from the nearest mainland, it is covered in nearly 900 monolithic carved figures with oversized heads, erected by Polynesian settlers. What is this island called in Rapa Nui?

options.info: Known internationally as Easter Island after the Dutch expedition that arrived on Easter Sunday 1722; its statues are the moai.
The Māori name for New Zealand, a very different Polynesian settlement.
An island in the Marquesas, part of the wider Polynesian world but not this one.
A real islet just off the coast of the correct answer, central to its birdman cult, but not the island itself.

question: Around 80% of it lies under an ice sheet up to three kilometres thick, its roughly 56,000 inhabitants are mostly Inuit, and it is a self-governing territory of a small European kingdom despite sitting on the North American plate. Which landmass?

options.info: The world's largest island, an autonomous territory of Denmark that left the European Communities in 1985.
The largest island in Canada and fifth largest in the world, but part of Nunavut rather than self-governing.
A Norwegian Arctic archipelago governed under a unique 1920 treaty, with no indigenous population.
A high Arctic Canadian island, heavily glaciated but far smaller and almost uninhabited.

question: Fed by one tributary rising in the Ethiopian highlands and another draining the Great Lakes region, this river's annual flood deposited the silt that made an ancient civilisation possible. Which river?

options.info: The Blue Nile and White Nile meet at Khartoum; the floods stopped after the Aswan High Dam was completed in 1970.
Africa's most powerful river by discharge, but it flows through rainforest, not desert farmland.
Takes a great arc through West Africa and floods into an inland delta in Mali.
Southern Africa's great river, best known for Victoria Falls.

question: Between 1405 and 1433 a Muslim eunuch admiral led seven enormous state fleets from China as far as Arabia and East Africa, bringing back tribute and, on one voyage, a giraffe for the emperor. Who commanded these treasure voyages?

options.info: His Ming dynasty fleets dwarfed anything in contemporary Europe; after his death the voyages were halted and the records largely destroyed.
Founded the Yuan dynasty and launched failed naval invasions of Japan, more than a century earlier.
The Ming emperor who ordered and funded the voyages, but did not sail on them.
A Moroccan traveller who covered even more ground, but as a lone wanderer rather than an admiral.

question: The first attempt that morning failed; the motorcade later took a wrong turn and reversed past a delicatessen where one of the conspirators happened to be standing. The two shots he fired set off the July Crisis of 1914. In which city?

options.info: Gavrilo Princip killed Archduke Franz Ferdinand and Sophie in the Bosnian capital on 28 June 1914.
The Serbian capital, target of Austria-Hungary's declaration of war a month later, but not the scene of the shooting.
Where the ultimatum to Serbia was drafted, and where the victims were buried.
Another Bosnian city, famous for its Ottoman bridge, but unconnected to the assassination.

question: A late-night safety test went badly wrong in April 1986, and Swedish workers detecting radiation on their clothes alerted the world before the Soviet authorities admitted anything. Near which town, in present-day Ukraine, did the reactor explode?

options.info: The reactor sat near the town of Pripyat, built for plant workers and evacuated 36 hours later; both lie in today's exclusion zone.
Site of the 1957 Kyshtym disaster in the Urals, a serious Soviet nuclear accident kept secret for decades.
Home to Europe's largest nuclear power station, but not the site of this accident.
A British nuclear site, scene of the 1957 Windscale fire.

question: Sailors once believed it dropped straight off the map's edge; today its highest waterfall plunges nearly a kilometre from a flat-topped tabletop mountain in Venezuela, mostly turning to mist before reaching the ground. What is that waterfall called?

options.info: Named after the American pilot Jimmie Angel, who crash-landed on the tepui above it in 1937; locally it is Kerepakupai Merú.
A spectacular horseshoe of hundreds of falls on the Argentina-Brazil border, far wider but much shorter.
A South African cascade sometimes claimed as the world's tallest, depending on how it is measured.
A single powerful drop in Guyana, on the same ancient highland shield but only about a quarter as tall.

question: Its logo is two Nordic runes laid on top of each other, and it was named after a 10th-century Scandinavian king who united warring tribes — chosen because the technology was meant to unite rival wireless standards. Which technology?

options.info: Named for King Harald 'Bluetooth' Gormsson of Denmark and Norway; the logo combines the runes for H and B.
A marketing name coined by a branding agency, with no meaning at all despite the 'wireless fidelity' myth.
Near Field Communication is a purely descriptive acronym with no royal namesake.
A low-power wireless standard named after the waggle dance of bees, not a monarch.

question: It is the second most expensive spice by weight, and outside its native Mexico the plant produced almost nothing for centuries until a 12-year-old enslaved boy on Réunion worked out how to pollinate the flowers by hand. Which flavouring?

options.info: It comes from the pods of a climbing orchid; Edmond Albius's 1841 hand-pollination method is still used on plantations today.
An expensive spice from a ginger relative, but native to South India and pollinated without human help.
Harvested as the inner bark of a tree, historically valuable but never dependent on hand pollination.
Once worth its weight in gold and native to the Banda Islands, but a seed rather than an orchid pod.

question: Its earliest known ancestor, chaturanga, had pieces representing infantry, cavalry, elephants and chariots, and spread west via Persia — which is why players still announce a Persian phrase meaning 'the king is helpless'. In which country did the game originate?

options.info: Chaturanga emerged in the Gupta era around the 6th century; 'checkmate' comes from the Persian 'shah mat'.
Adapted the game as shatranj and passed it to the Arab world, but did not invent it.
Has its own ancient board game, xiangqi, whose relationship to this one is still debated.
Played the ancient board game senet, unrelated to this one.

question: The story goes that an 18th-century English aristocrat, unwilling to leave the gambling table for a proper meal, asked for meat served between two slices of bread. What was his title, now attached to the snack?

options.info: John Montagu, 4th Earl of Sandwich; Captain Cook also named the Sandwich Islands (Hawaii) after him as his naval patron.
Lends his name to beef Wellington, a completely different dish.
A 19th-century prime minister whose name attached to a bergamot-scented tea.
A later British prime minister; 'Salisbury steak' is actually named after an American physician instead.

question: In 1951 a managing director missed a shot on a bird-shooting trip and then argued in the pub about which European game bird was fastest — discovering no book existed to settle it. Which company was he running, and duly gave its name to the book he commissioned?

options.info: Sir Hugh Beaver commissioned the record book in 1954 as a giveaway to settle pub arguments; it became a bestseller in its own right.
Another historic British brewery, holder of the UK's first registered trademark, but not behind this book.
A major British brewer that sponsored a literary prize and a round-the-world yacht race instead.
A Danish brewery famous for funding a scientific laboratory, not a record book.

question: He was a palace guard in Addis Ababa and only got a place in the 1960 Rome Olympic marathon because a teammate broke an ankle weeks beforehand. The shoes he was issued gave him blisters, so he ran the entire race barefoot over Roman cobblestones and finished under the floodlit Arch of Constantine in world-record time. Who was he?

options.info: He won again in Tokyo in 1964, this time in shoes and just weeks after an appendectomy — the first man to take back-to-back Olympic marathons.
His compatriot and training partner, who won the Olympic marathon at Mexico City in 1968.
A track and marathon great of the 1990s and 2000s, with two Olympic 10,000m titles.
Holder of world records over 5,000m and 10,000m for well over a decade, born long after 1960.

question: Despite the New York neighbourhood in their name, this exhibition basketball team was actually founded in Chicago in the 1920s — the name was chosen to signal who the players were and to sound like a team that had already travelled. They turned ball-handling tricks and comedy routines into a global touring act, and for decades faced the same obliging opponents night after night. Which team?

options.info: Their long-suffering opposition, the Washington Generals, lost thousands of games — but genuinely beat them in 1971 when a routine ran late.
A dominant New York barnstorming side of the 1920s, but a straight competitive team rather than a comedy act.
The great Black professional team of the 1920s and 30s, named after a Harlem ballroom, who played to win.
An early 20th-century American amateur powerhouse, long gone by the time exhibition touring took off.

question: An Austrian zoologist spent years watching marked honeybees on glass-walled hives and worked out that a forager returning with news of food walks a figure-of-eight on the vertical comb, waggling through the straight middle section. The angle of that straight run away from vertical, he found, matches the angle of the food source away from the sun. What does the length of that waggling run tell the watching bees?

options.text: How far away the food is
options.info: Roughly speaking, a longer waggle means a longer flight — about one extra second per kilometre. Karl von Frisch shared a Nobel Prize for decoding it in 1973.
Enthusiasm and repetition do signal quality, but the duration of the straight run specifically encodes distance.

options.text: How many bees are needed to harvest it
options.info: Recruitment scales with how many bees follow the dance, not with any figure encoded in its timing.

options.text: What time of day the flowers open
options.info: Bees really do learn flower timetables, but they do it individually rather than by broadcasting it in the dance.

question: When a preserved specimen reached London in 1799, naturalists assumed a taxidermist somewhere in Asia had stitched a hoax together and went looking for the stitches. The animal turned out to be real: it lays eggs, oozes milk through the skin instead of feeding through nipples, shuts its eyes, ears and nostrils underwater and hunts by sensing the electrical twitch of prey through its bill, and the males carry venomous spurs on their hind legs. Which animal is it?

options.info: Found only in eastern Australia and Tasmania. Its venom is agonising to humans and reportedly does not respond to morphine.
The only other egg-laying mammal alive today, and it also has a spur — but the male's is not venomous, and it eats ants and termites.
The scaly, ant-eating mammal of Africa and Asia — extraordinary, but it gives birth to live young.
A Madagascan lemur that taps on wood and fishes out grubs with a skeletal middle finger; also a placental mammal.

question: Handed out with the bill in almost every Chinese restaurant in the United States, one of these items is essentially unknown in China itself — when an American company tried selling them in Hong Kong in the 1990s, they were marketed as an exotic foreign novelty and flopped. Food historians instead trace it to Japanese immigrant bakeries and tea gardens in California around 1900. Which item is it?

options.info: A similar folded cracker with a slip of paper inside was sold near Kyoto long before; Chinese-American restaurants adopted it during the Second World War.
Also an American-Chinese creation rather than a Chinese dish, but it came from Cantonese immigrant cooks, not Japanese bakers.
Invented by a Hunanese chef in Taiwan in the 1950s and then sweetened heavily for New York diners.
A thicker American cousin of the Chinese spring roll, standardised in New York restaurants in the 1930s.

question: In August 1945, with Soviet troops already moving south, two American colonels were given half an hour to propose where a peninsula should be divided. Working from a small-scale National Geographic map, they picked a line of latitude that kept the capital on the American side. The strip either side of the 1953 armistice line is now about four kilometres wide, heavily mined, and — because almost nobody has walked in for seventy years — an accidental wildlife refuge for cranes and possibly leopards. Which parallel did they choose?

options.info: One of the two officers, Dean Rusk, later became US Secretary of State. The actual armistice line of 1953 wanders either side of it.
The line that divided Vietnam after the 1954 Geneva Accords — a similar improvisation, a different peninsula.

question: Released in 1940 while the United States was still neutral, this film had its writer-director playing both a persecuted Jewish barber and a ranting dictator called Adenoid Hynkel — and it was his first picture with full dialogue, after decades of resisting sound. Who made it?

options.info: 'The Great Dictator' was his highest-grossing film; he later said he could not have made the comedy had he known the full extent of the camps.
The other great silent clown, famed for stone-faced stunts, whose career had faded badly by 1940.
A silent comedy star best remembered dangling from a clock face, but not the maker of this film.
Directed his own Nazi-mocking comedy, 'To Be or Not to Be', two years later.
